unresolved_must_fix.claim: The revision cut Eugene raising Hercules for the pagans but kept 'society on both sides' and 'boxing-match'. The contest between divine powers now has no second fighter.
unresolved_must_fix.counterevidence: 'Rival' implies opposition, but nothing marks Eugene as the pagan champion.

evidence.quote: and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match
and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match.
Theodosius marched against his rival Eugene with the Cross for physical champion; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match.

unresolved_must_fix.minimal_repair: Restore 'and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans;' or cut the Theodosius sentence entirely.
unresolved_must_fix.plan_relation: optional tradeoff (Theodosius trimmable), but the residue is not excused
unresolved_must_fix.reader_effect: The image of a test of force between Cross and pagan god collapses. The plan allowed trimming Theodosius, not a dangling residue.
unresolved_must_fix.title: Boxing-match left with only one contender

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The sentence contrasting a costly machine with hiring an occult force at trifling expense was cut. 'Fetish-power was cheap' now stands as bare assertion at the head of the slave/fetish argument.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: The slave-machine comparison that follows partly implies the point.

evidence.quote: no one could afford to buy or construct a costly and complicated machine when he could hire an occult force at trifling expense.
No one could afford to buy or construct a costly and complicated machine when he could hire an occult force at trifling expense.
Fetish-power was cheap and satisfactory, down to a certain point. Outside of it, the Roman world was incredibly poor.

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's one sentence before 'Fetish-power was cheap'.
unresolved_should_improve.plan_relation: required (slave and fetish as Rome's only engines)
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: It weakens the economic logic of Rome's 'only engines' and the vicious circle that follows.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Why fetish-power was 'cheap' is no longer argued

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The revision cut society's disappointment that the Cross 'had failed to protect its Church'. 'The outcry against the Cross' is now unmotivated. It also cut the Civitas Dei becoming the new 'sum of attraction' with the same mechanical weakness.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: The sack of Rome immediately precedes, so a reader can infer the cause.

evidence.quote: The Civitas Dei, in its turn, became the sum of attraction for the Western world, though it also showed the same weakness in mechanics
Society felt still more deeply the disappointment in its new power, the Cross, which had failed to protect its Church.
The outcry against the Cross became so loud among Christians that Bishop Augustine of Hippo was led to write a famous treatise in defence of the Cross

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's 'failed to protect its Church' sentence and its Civitas Dei sentence.
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: The Cross-as-fetish argument loses its test case. The bridge to 'Yet the attraction remained constant' and the Middle Ages is weaker.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Outcry against the Cross and the Civitas Dei hinge lost

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The revision removed the claim that the two forces 'seemed to drop from the sky' just as the Cross and Crescent proclaimed the triumph of the Civitas Dei. It also cut the Eastern Empire's 'activity and variety of forces'.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: 'Sudden, unexplained appearance' keeps the abruptness, and 'forces not quite the same' gestures at Byzantium.

evidence.quote: Literally, these two forces seemed to drop from the sky at the precise moment when the Cross on one side and the Crescent
The Eastern Empire showed an activity and variety of forces that classical Europe had never possessed.
he is distinctly conscious of forces not quite the same. The dynamic scheme began by asserting rather recklessly

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Restore the 'Literally... Civitas Dei' sentence and the Eastern Empire sentence, both present in the first draft.
unresolved_should_improve.plan_relation: required (Byzantium; sudden arrival of the new forces)
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: This loses the paradox that sets up 'diabolic' explosives and the 'battle... between gunpowder and the Cross'. The plan's 'Byzantium shows more varied forces' survives only as a vague hint.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Ironic timing of the new forces and Byzantine variety cut

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The revision cut 'dragged into situations... anarchic', the fish-on-a-hook image, Bacon's instruments paragraph, and the 'long series of groups, dragged on' that 'even the leaders obeyed without understanding'. 'This method' now follows the Franklin sentence without its Baconian antecedent.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: 'The Baconian law held good' in p22 can serve loosely as the referent of 'method'.

evidence.quote: dragged on by an attractive power in advance, which even the leaders obeyed without understanding
Europe saw itself, violently resisting, drawn along new lines as a fish that is caught on a hook

unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: The thesis that acceleration was involuntary and uncomprehended rests mostly on 'mechanical as the fall of a feather'. 'Resistance' lacks its dragging counterforce.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Post-1500 involuntariness thinned; 'this method' dangles
